topics.title: How to Keep Score
topics.summary: The three numbers, side-outs, and why you only score on your serve.

sections.heading: The basics
sections.body: Games are played to 11 points and you must win by 2. Only the serving team can score a point — if the receiving team wins the rally, no point is scored; instead the serve changes hands (a side-out in singles, or the next server in doubles).

sections.heading: Doubles: the three numbers
sections.body: The score is called as three numbers: your team's score, the other team's score, then the server number (1 or 2). Example: "4–2–1" means your team has 4, they have 2, and you're the first server. Both players on a team get to serve before the serve passes to the other team — except at the very start of the game.

sections.heading: Why games start at 0–0–2
sections.body: To offset the advantage of serving first, the team that serves first only gets ONE server for their first turn. That first server is called "2", so the game starts at 0–0–2. When they lose a rally, the serve goes straight to the other team.

sections.heading: When do we switch sides of our own court?
sections.body: You and your partner swap left/right sides every time your team scores a point while serving. If your score is even, the first server of the game stands on the right; odd, on the left. If nobody has scored since your team got the serve, nobody moves.

sections.heading: Singles
sections.body: Same idea without server numbers: call your score, then your opponent's. Serve from the right side when your score is even, the left when it's odd.

topics.title: Serving Rules
topics.summary: Underhand, behind the baseline, diagonal — and the drop serve option.

sections.heading: The legal serve
sections.body: Serve underhand with the paddle moving in an upward arc, making contact below your waist with the paddle head below your wrist. Both feet must be behind the baseline, and the serve travels diagonally cross-court into the opposite service box, clearing the kitchen and the kitchen line.

sections.heading: The drop serve (easier!)
sections.body: You may instead drop the ball from any height (no throwing it down) and hit it after the bounce. The paddle restrictions don't apply to the drop serve, which makes it a great option while you're learning.

sections.heading: One try
sections.body: You get one serve attempt. If it lands in the kitchen, hits the net and lands short, or misses the box, it's a fault and the serve moves on. (A serve that clips the net but lands in the correct box is a live "let" — you play it.)

sections.heading: Where to aim
sections.body: Deep. A serve that lands in the back third of the box keeps your opponent pinned at the baseline and makes their third shot harder. Consistency beats power — get every serve in before you worry about pace.

topics.title: The Kitchen (Non-Volley Zone)
topics.summary: The 7-foot zone where you can't volley — pickleball's most misunderstood rule.

sections.heading: What it is
sections.body: The kitchen is the 7-foot zone on each side of the net (officially the non-volley zone). You may stand in it any time you like — what you may NOT do is hit a volley (a ball out of the air, before it bounces) while touching it.

sections.heading: The details that catch people
sections.body: The kitchen line counts as part of the kitchen. If your momentum after a volley carries you into the kitchen — even a toe on the line, even after the ball is dead — it's a fault. If the ball bounces first, you can step in and hit it from inside the kitchen legally.

sections.heading: Why it exists
sections.body: Without it, tall players would stand at the net and smash everything. The kitchen forces the soft game — dinks, drops, and resets — which is where pickleball strategy lives.

sections.heading: Playing around it
sections.body: Stand just behind the kitchen line, toes an inch or two back. Volley anything you can reach; let anything soft bounce, then step in and dink it back. After hitting a ball that bounced in the kitchen, step back out so you're ready to volley the next one.

topics.title: The Two-Bounce Rule
topics.summary: Why you can't rush the net right away.

sections.heading: The rule
sections.body: After the serve, the ball must bounce once on each side before anyone may volley. The receiving team must let the serve bounce, and the serving team must let the return bounce. From the third shot on, volleys are allowed (outside the kitchen).

sections.heading: What it means for you
sections.body: The serving team should stay back at the baseline until they've hit the third shot — if you creep forward, the return will bounce at your feet. The receiver's partner can already stand at the kitchen line; the receiver moves up right after returning.

topics.title: Common Faults
topics.summary: The ways a rally ends — and the ones beginners forget.

sections.heading: The obvious ones
sections.body: Hitting the ball into the net or out of bounds, letting it bounce twice, or missing the serve. A ball landing ON a line is in — except the kitchen line on a serve, which is a fault.

sections.heading: The sneaky ones
sections.body: Volleying while touching the kitchen or its line (including momentum afterward). Volleying the serve or the return before it bounces (two-bounce rule). Touching the net, or the ball touching you or your clothing during a rally. Serving from the wrong side or when it isn't your serve.

sections.heading: Etiquette worth knowing
sections.body: You call lines on your own side, and the benefit of the doubt goes to your opponent. If the ball hits you — even on a winning shot — it's their point. Announce the score clearly before every serve; it prevents most arguments before they start.

topics.title: Where to Stand
topics.summary: Court positioning basics: the kitchen line is home.

sections.heading: The golden rule
sections.body: Points are won at the kitchen line. Whichever team gets both players established there first usually wins the rally — that's the entire reason the third-shot drop exists.

sections.heading: Serving team
sections.body: Both players start at the baseline and STAY there until the third shot is struck (the return has to bounce on your side). Hit a drop or drive, then advance together — through the transition zone, splitting your steps as the opponents hit.

sections.heading: Receiving team
sections.body: The receiver's partner starts at the kitchen line. The receiver returns deep, then follows the return forward. Done right, the receiving team owns the net before the serving team has even moved.

sections.heading: Move as a pair
sections.body: In doubles, imagine a rope between you and your partner. Slide left and right together, following the ball, so there's never a wide-open gap in the middle. If your partner gets pulled wide, you shift to cover the middle.

topics.title: Choosing Your First Paddle
topics.summary: What actually matters when you're starting out — and what doesn't.

sections.heading: Don't overspend
sections.body: A mid-priced composite or fiberglass paddle is all a new player needs. Expensive carbon paddles reward skills you haven't built yet. Spend the difference on a bucket of outdoor balls and court time.

sections.heading: What to look for
sections.body: Weight around 7.5–8.2 oz — light enough for quick hands at the net, heavy enough for drives. A standard shape with a large sweet spot beats an elongated paddle for beginners. Grip size: with the paddle in hand, you should fit an index finger between your fingertips and palm.

sections.heading: Balls are not all the same
sections.body: Outdoor balls are harder with smaller holes; indoor balls are softer with bigger holes. They play very differently — practice with the type your local courts use.

sections.heading: Shoes matter more than paddles
sections.body: Running shoes are built for straight lines and will roll an ankle on lateral movement. Court shoes (tennis, volleyball, or pickleball-specific) are the single best equipment upgrade a new player can make.

topics.title: Dinking & the Soft Game
topics.summary: Why soft shots win rallies — and how to stop losing them with hard ones.

sections.heading: Why soft wins
sections.body: At the kitchen line, a hard shot at a ready opponent comes back harder. A dink they have to hit from below net height can't be attacked — it can only be dinked back. The soft game isn't passive; it's how you force the mistake or the pop-up you get to put away.

sections.heading: How to dink
sections.body: Bend your knees, keep the paddle out in front, and push gently from the shoulder — no wrist flick. Aim to land the ball in the kitchen, low enough that it would clip the net if your opponent tried to attack it. Height control matters more than placement at first.

sections.heading: Patience is a skill
sections.body: Most beginner points end with someone speeding up a ball they shouldn't have. If the dink coming at you is low, dink it back — even ten times in a row. Attack only when the ball sits up above net height. Counting rallies in practice ("can we get to 20?") builds the habit.

sections.heading: From banging to placing
sections.body: Players from tennis or racquetball start by hitting hard at everything — and it works, until opponents learn to block. The upgrade path is the same for everyone: learn the dink, then the third-shot drop, then the reset. Power still matters, but as a surprise, not a default.

topics.title: Doubles Positioning & Communication
topics.summary: Move as a unit, cover the middle, and say what you're doing out loud.

sections.heading: The invisible rope
sections.body: Imagine a 10-foot rope tying you to your partner. When they slide wide, you slide with them; when they move up, you move up. Two players moving independently leave a hole in the middle — and the middle is where good opponents aim.

sections.heading: Who takes the middle?
sections.body: Default: the player with their forehand in the middle takes middle balls. Decide before the game starts and say it out loud. When in doubt, the player who hit the last shot crossing the middle usually keeps it — but any agreement beats silence.

sections.heading: Talk constantly
sections.body: "Mine." "Yours." "Bounce it." "Out!" "Switch." One-word calls prevent both the collision and the ball nobody touched. Calling "out" on a flying ball is helping your partner duck — it isn't a line call until it lands.

sections.heading: When your partner gets lobbed
sections.body: Don't watch — cross behind them. The player who can see the lob best (the one NOT under it) calls "switch", covers the lobbed side, and their partner fills the vacated side. Practice it once and it becomes automatic.

topics.title: Understanding Ratings & DUPR
topics.summary: What the numbers mean, how they move, and why this app asks for a target.

sections.heading: What DUPR is
sections.body: DUPR (Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating) scores every player on one scale from about 2.0 to 5.0+, based on match results — who you played and how close the game was. You don't need an official rating to use this app: a self-estimate (or the 60-second skill check) is enough to start.

sections.heading: How the tiers feel
sections.body: 2.0 New to the Game: learning to serve, return, and keep score. 2.5 Advanced Beginner: short rallies, knows the basic rules. 3.0 Beginner: consistent strokes, learning court positioning. 3.5 Intermediate: third-shot drops, kitchen game, transitions. 4.0 Advanced: pattern recognition, speed-up and reset battles. 5.0 Pro: tournament-level tactics.

sections.heading: How ratings move
sections.body: Official DUPR updates after recorded matches — rec games count if players log them, and tournaments count automatically. Beating a higher-rated player moves you up faster than beating a lower-rated one. Expect slow movement: a half-point jump usually represents months of play.

sections.heading: Why the app asks for a target
sections.body: Your target rating tells the AI which skills to train next. A 3.0 player targeting 3.5 gets drills for the exact skills that separate those tiers — drops, kitchen play, transitions — instead of generic practice. Set the target one tier above your current level and re-take the skill check as you improve.

topics.title: Pickleball Etiquette
topics.summary: The unwritten rules: open play, line calls, and not being that player.

sections.heading: Open-play rotation
sections.body: Most public courts run paddle-stack rotation: finished players stack their paddles by the gate and the next four in line take the court. Games are usually to 11, win by 1 at busy sessions. Winners staying on varies by venue — watch what the locals do or just ask.

sections.heading: Score first, then serve
sections.body: Call all three numbers loudly BEFORE you start your serving motion. It keeps everyone honest, prevents most arguments, and is required by the rules anyway. If you've lost track, ask — nobody minds.

sections.heading: Line calls and benefit of the doubt
sections.body: You call the lines on your side, and "if you're not sure, it's in." Never call a ball on your opponent's side unless they ask. Overruling your own partner's call in your favor is bad form; overruling it in the opponent's favor is good form.

sections.heading: Ball on court!
sections.body: If a ball rolls onto your court, stop the rally immediately by calling "ball on" — replay the point. If your ball rolls toward another court, shout it just as fast; a ball underfoot mid-rally is how ankles get broken. And after every game, win or lose: paddle taps at the net.

topics.title: Warming Up & Staying Injury-Free
topics.summary: Five minutes of prep that keeps you on the court all season.

sections.heading: The five-minute warm-up
sections.body: Before the first game: a minute of light jogging or jumping jacks, leg swings front-to-back and side-to-side, arm circles, and a few gentle lunges. Then dink cross-court for a couple of minutes before hitting anything hard. Cold-starting with drives is how elbows and shoulders get cranky.

sections.heading: Never backpedal for a lob
sections.body: Backpedaling with your eyes up is the single most common cause of serious pickleball falls. When a lob goes over you, turn sideways, run back like you're chasing a fly ball, then set up to hit. If you can't get there — let it bounce or let your partner cross. No point is worth the back of your head.

sections.heading: Gear that prevents injuries
sections.body: Court shoes over running shoes, always — lateral support is everything. Eye protection is cheap insurance at the kitchen line, where speed-ups arrive fast from ten feet away. If your elbow complains, check your grip size and paddle weight before blaming your swing.

sections.heading: Listen to the niggles
sections.body: Pickleball is addictive and most injuries are overuse: play three days in a row and your knees will file a complaint. Hydrate, cool down with easy stretching for calves, shoulders, and forearms, and take the rest day. Missing one session beats missing a month.

glossary.definition: A soft shot from at or near the kitchen line that lands in the opponent's kitchen, too low to attack.
A soft shot by the serving team on the third shot of the rally, arcing into the opponent's kitchen so the servers can advance to the net.
A hard, flat groundstroke — the aggressive alternative to a drop on the third shot.
Hitting the ball out of the air before it bounces. Illegal while touching the kitchen or its line.
Nickname for the non-volley zone: the 7-foot area on each side of the net where volleying is not allowed.
After the serve, the ball must bounce once on each side before anyone may volley.
When the serve passes to the other team after the serving team loses the rally (or both servers lose it, in doubles).
A defensive soft shot that takes the pace off a hard ball and drops it into the kitchen, neutralizing an attack.
Deliberately hitting a fast, aggressive shot out of a slow dink rally to catch the opponent off guard.
An advanced volley hit from outside the court, next to the kitchen, letting you take the ball out of the air close to the net legally.
A shot hit around the outside of the net post — legal at any height, since it never crosses the net.
A doubles formation where partners line up on the same side before the serve so each ends up on their preferred half of the court.
The mid-court area between the baseline and the kitchen line — a place to pass through carefully, not to camp in.
A small hop onto both feet as your opponent strikes the ball, keeping you balanced and ready to move either way.
A serve that clips the net but still lands in the correct service box — it's live, play it.
Dynamic Universal Pickleball Rating — the rating system this app uses. Roughly 2.0 for brand-new players up to 5.0+ for pros.
Crossing into your partner's side to take a ball out of the air — aggressive, and best announced or pre-planned so nobody collides.
A high, deep shot over the opponents' heads, pushing them off the kitchen line. Chase it by turning and running — never backpedaling.
A hard downward shot on a ball above your head — the usual answer to a short lob.
An Erne hit in front of your PARTNER's side of the court — leaping across to volley beside the kitchen. Advanced and flashy.
A doubles play: one partner drives the third shot while the other crashes the net to put away the pop-up.
A short, firm volley pushed from the shoulder with almost no backswing — the bread-and-butter volley at the kitchen line.
The tilt of your paddle at contact. Open (tilted up) lifts the ball — good for dinks; closed (tilted down) drives it low.
An alternate format where a point is scored on every rally, whoever served. Used in some rec play and pro doubles — traditional side-out scoring is still the default.
Stepping on or inside the baseline while serving, or touching the kitchen (or its line) on a volley — both lose the rally.
A speed-up aimed at an opponent's torso or paddle-side hip, where it's hardest to defend. If the ball hits any part of you, the point is theirs.
